senses.gloss:
dhātuprasāda
(‘by the grace of धातु’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term that appears only in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad (1.2.20).
While describing the nature of the आत्मन् (the Self), यम declares that he is smaller than the smallest as also greater than the greatest. He is established in the cave of the heart of all living beings.
One who realizes him and his greatness becomes free from all sorrow and suffering.
This is preceded by two conditions: to be akratu and to receive धातुप्रसाद.
To become an akratu or free from volition, the aspirant should avoid all desires and desire-motivated actions. Not being agitated thus by desires, his मिन्द् and senses which are called धातु since they support the living beings, become propitious unto him. This is धातुप्रसाद.
However, the भक्ति schools of Vedānta interpret the word ‘dhātuprasādāt’ as ‘by the grace of परमात्मन् or God’. So, the जीव or the individual सोउल् is able to understand the greatness of God through his grace and thus transcends all sorrow.
This verse is repeated in the Śvetā-śvatara (3.20) and Mahānārāyaṇa (8.3) उपनिषद्स् also.

dhātu
(‘that which exists [in all]’)
------------------------------------------
This word is used in several senses. In the darśanas or treatises on philosophy it stands for the पञ्चभूतस् or the five elements, viz., earth, water, fire, air and sky (or space or ether).
In the ancient medical sciences, seven dhātus which sustain our body (‘sapta-dhātus’) are mentioned. They are: रस (chyle), asṛk or rakta (blood), māṁsa (flesh), medas (fat), asthi (bone), majjā (marrow) and शुक्र (semen).
Metals dug out from the bowels of earth like gold and silver as also precious stones are also known as ‘dhātu’.
In Sanskrit grammar, the word means the root form of a verb, like bhū (= to exist).
